content: The following hygiene kit components can be considered for individuals with lymphedema, depending on the available budget: unscented soap, towels or gauze, antibacterial cream, antifungal cream, antiseptics, a basin, a bucket, a cup, suitable shoes, and patient education materials. Community health workers should be involved whenever possible to support patients and families in maintaining lymphedema management practices and to refer patients for further care, such as treatment for episodes of acute dermatolymphangioadenitis (ADL), when necessary. In areas where Brugia species are present, patients should be educated on proper abscess dressing techniques, as infections with these species increase the risk of abscesses on the proximal limbs. Hydrocele, a condition associated with LF, can be effectively treated through hydrocelectomy surgery in health facilities equipped to perform the procedure. The expected outcomes of surgery include a return to normal or reduced scrotal size, improved quality of life, and enhanced patient functionality. WHO consultations in 2002 and 2017 reviewed and revised surgical approaches to hydrocele management, emphasizing the importance of standard operating procedures and harmonizing these with other surgical initiatives. Surgery is recommended for all stages of hydrocele, including small hydroceles, to prevent progression to more severe and difficult-to-treat stages. Hydrocelectomy has been identified as one of the 28 essential surgical procedures that should be available at first-level health facilities worldwide. The choice of surgical technique for hydrocelectomy depends on the practices of the local surgical service and factors such as the capacity of local facilities, patient risk factors, and the stage or grade of the hydrocele. The Capuano and Capuano hydrocele grading system has been adopted to standardize indicators across settings and guide stratified management. For uncomplicated hydroceles (Stages I–III), surgery can typically be performed at Level I or II facilities, while complicated hydroceles (Stages III–VI) often require specialized surgical teams at Level III facilities. The excision technique, performed with electrocautery by experienced surgeons, is preferred. Pre-operative antibiotics are usually sufficient for uncomplicated cases, while antibiotic regimens for complicated cases should be tailored based on pre-operative skin cultures, scrotal skin thickness, and other patient factors. Hydrocelectomy should be conducted in a proper operating room equipped with oxygen, adequate lighting, suction, an electrocautery machine (if available), patient monitoring equipment, and resuscitation medications. Surgical teams are encouraged to use the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist to improve safety and reduce complications. Preand post-operative preparation and support are critical to the success of the intervention. Pre-operatively, a comprehensive physical exam, including ultrasound, should confirm the diagnosis and identify complicating features. Post-operatively, patients should be observed on-site for at least 72 hours to monitor for infection and change dressings. Hydrocelectomy camps can play a role in treating large numbers of patients quickly and strengthening local surgical capacity. However, these camps should not replace efforts to strengthen local access to surgical care, as they may strain local resources and staff. Instead, they should complement broader health system strengthening efforts. Antifilarial drug treatment is recommended for individuals who test positive for filarial antigen or microfilariae to eliminate the parasites. However, many patients with filarial lymphedema or hydrocele may test negative for microfilariae or filarial antigen and do not require antifilarial medications. Limited evidence suggests that a 4–6 week course of doxycycline (200 mg per day) may stabilize or reverse disease progression in lymphedema patients. Ongoing clinical trials are evaluating the effectiveness of doxycycline as a management strategy, and WHO will update recommendations based on the results. Strategic planning for morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP) is essential for achieving the global goal of providing access to care for all individuals with LF-related conditions. WHO's strategic plan for 2021–2030 emphasizes integrating quality services for LF morbidity management into national health systems, training health staff, and strengthening referral mechanisms. The ultimate aim is to achieve 100% geographic coverage of the minimum package of care, including lymphedema management, ADL treatment, and hydrocelectomy, through the health system at appropriate levels. National programs are encouraged to conduct situation analyses to estimate the number of lymphedema and hydrocele patients, assess health system capacity, and identify gaps in policy and resources. Advocacy, social mobilization, and community engagement are critical components of these efforts.
